lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: So you finally made it down here too, Polystratus. You must have lived, what, not much short of a hundred years?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Ninety-eight, Simylus.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: And how was life for those thirty years after me? I died when you were about seventy.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Extremely pleasant. Though I can see why that may surprise you.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: It does. Old, weak, childless on top of it — and you could still enjoy being alive?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: First of all, I could enjoy everything. There were handsome boys, plenty of them; very delicate ladies; perfumes; wine with a bouquet on it; and dinners better than anything in Sicily.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: This is new. I knew you as a very careful man with money.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Ah, but the good things came pouring in from other people, my excellent friend. From dawn onward, crowds were at my door; then gifts were brought to me from everywhere on earth — always the finest available.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Did you become a tyrant after I died, Polystratus?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: No. I had lovers. Thousands of them.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: [laughs] Lovers? You? At that age? With four teeth?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: By Zeus, yes — the best men in the city. Old as I was, bald as you see me, bleary-eyed besides, and running at the nose, they adored waiting on me. The man I so much as glanced at thought himself blessed.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: What happened, then? Like Phaon, did you ferry Aphrodite over from Chios, say the right prayer, and get turned young and beautiful again — irresistible from scratch?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: No. I was irresistible exactly as I was.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: You are speaking in riddles.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Not really. This particular passion is perfectly obvious: the very strong love people feel for rich old men with no children.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: Now I understand your beauty, my marvelous friend. It came from Golden Aphrodite.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: In any case, Simylus, I had no small profit out of my lovers. They practically worshipped me. Often I played the spoiled darling; sometimes I shut some of them out. Then they competed, each trying to outdo the other in devotion to me.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: And in the end, what did you decide about the property?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Publicly, I told each of them I was leaving him my heir. Each one believed it, naturally, and made himself even more flatteringly useful. But I had another will, the real one. I left that behind, and gave them all notice to howl.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: And who was heir in the final will? Someone from your family, I suppose?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: No, by Zeus. A Phrygian boy I had recently bought. A pretty one.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: About how old, Polystratus?

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Around twenty.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: I am beginning to understand what services he performed for you.

lines.speaker: Polystratus
lines.text: Still, he deserved the inheritance far more than the others did — even if he was a barbarian and a little ruin of a creature. The same finest gentlemen now pay court to him. So he inherited from me, and now he is counted among the aristocrats: chin shaved, accent barbarous, yet said to be nobler than Codrus, prettier than Nireus, and cleverer than Odysseus.

lines.speaker: Simylus
lines.text: I don't care. Let him command all Greece, if he likes — provided those people do not inherit.
